course.title: Calculus: Change and Accumulation
course.description: Bring points together, trace a tangent and build an area. Discover how change accumulates.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with algebra, function notation, powers and coordinate graphs. This introductory course develops polynomial limits, rates and accumulation.

paragraphs: Calculus is the mathematics of change, and it rests on two questions that algebra cannot answer on its own: how fast a quantity is changing at one exact moment, and how much has built up after a stretch of change. Engineers use it to design bridges and engines, scientists to model motion, growth and heat, and economists to follow how costs and profits shift, and anyone who goes on to physics, statistics or machine learning meets it early.

The course has twelve lessons in four parts, and each part builds on the one before. The first begins with the limit, which gives a meaning to a fraction that reads 0 ÷ 0 at a point, and ends with the derivative, the slope of a curve at a single point. The second gives rules for finding derivatives quickly, including the chain rule for a function placed inside another, and applies them to motion. The third uses derivatives to find where a curve turns, runs them backwards to recover a function from its rate, and builds an area from thin rectangles. The fourth gives areas a sign and shows that the derivative and the integral undo each other, which is the fundamental theorem of calculus.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, so a question comes only after you have been shown what it needs.
outcomes: You'll be able to find a limit by simplifying a fraction, and say when a graph has a break.
You'll be able to find the slope of a curve at a point, from a limit and with the power and chain rules.
You'll be able to read speed and acceleration from a position, and find where a curve turns.
You'll be able to estimate an area with rectangles and find it exactly with an antiderivative.
You'll be able to explain how the fundamental theorem links rates to totals, and use it to find net change.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with algebra, function notation, powers and graphs on coordinate axes.

steps.headline: As the input closes in on 2 from either side, the output closes in on 4

lead.text: The input 2 is not allowed, but nothing prevents us from going as near to it as we like. Start on the left, with x = 1.5: the top is 1.5² − 4, which is −1.75, the bottom is 1.5 − 2, which is −0.5, and the output is 3.5. Moving closer, x = 1.9 gives 3.9 and x = 1.99 gives 3.99, so **every step towards 2 brings the output a step nearer to 4**.
The same thing happens from the other side. The inputs 2.5, 2.1 and 2.01 give outputs of 4.5, 4.1 and 4.01, which fall towards 4 while the inputs fall towards 2.

afterFigure.text: What matters is that **the two walks end at the same place**. Inputs from the left and from the right both lead the output to 4, so the graph behaves as though it were about to pass through height 4 at x = 2, even though the point itself is missing. Nothing in the table required the fraction to have a value at 2; it required only values *near* 2.

steps.headline: The limit is the value the outputs approach, whatever happens at the point itself

lead.text: The number the outputs are closing in on is called the **limit** of the fraction as x approaches 2, and it is written with the abbreviation lim:

A limit describes where the outputs *head*. It makes **no claim about an output at the point itself**, which is why this limit can exist when the fraction has no value at 2. Not every point has a gap, however. The function h(x) = 10 − x is defined at 4, where it gives 6, and as x approaches 4 its outputs approach 6 as well. The figure shows both graphs, and the slider on each brings a pair of points closer to the point of interest from the two sides.

afterFigure.text: The idea was in use long before it had a careful definition. Newton and Leibniz built calculus in the later seventeenth century on quantities that were allowed to shrink towards nothing, and it was Augustin-Louis Cauchy who, in his *Cours d'analyse* of 1821, described a limit as the fixed value that a variable's successive values approach until they differ from it as little as one wishes.

lead.text: To read a [[limit|The value the outputs approach as the input approaches a point. Met earlier in this lesson.]] from a table, look at where **the outputs are going** and ignore where the inputs happen to be standing. The next question gives the outputs of a simpler function at three inputs and asks where they lead.
The fraction (x² − 9)/(x − 3) has the same kind of gap as the first one, this time at x = 3. Take one output from the right of the gap, at x = 3.1, and work it out in full.

steps.headline: A fraction that reads 0 ÷ 0 at the point can often be simplified

lead.text: A table is slow, and it only suggests an answer, but the first table was quietly pointing to a faster route. Every output in it was the input plus 2: 1.5 gave 3.5, 1.9 gave 3.9 and 2.5 gave 4.5. That is no coincidence, because the top of the fraction is a [[difference of squares|a² − b² factors as (a − b)(a + b).]], so x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2), and for every x except 2 the factor x − 2 on top cancels the x − 2 below, leaving x + 2.

Putting x = 2 straight into the original fraction gives 0 ÷ 0, which is called an **indeterminate form**, because it does not determine a value. The fractions 3x/x and 7x/x both read 0 ÷ 0 at x = 0, yet they approach 3 and 7, so the form alone cannot say what a quotient does near the point. It is a signal to *rewrite* the fraction, and the plan is to **factor, cancel what can be cancelled, and then ask what the simplified expression approaches**.

steps.headline: Limit of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) as x approaches 3

lead.text: You worked out this fraction at x = 3.1 a moment ago. Here is its limit at 3, found by **factoring and cancelling**, which replaces a table of values with *a single argument*.

workedSteps.text: Putting x = 3 into the fraction gives 0 ÷ 0, an [[indeterminate form|A fraction of the form 0 ÷ 0, which does not determine a value. Met earlier in this lesson.]], which settles nothing, so the fraction has to be rewritten.
The top is a difference of squares, so it factors, and the factor x − 3 now stands above and below.
Cancel the factor x − 3.
What remains has no gap, so let x approach 3 in it. The result agrees with the 6.1 found at x = 3.1, which sits a little above 6 because 3.1 is a little above 3.

steps.headline: Limit of (x² − 49)/(x − 7) as x approaches 7

lead.text: The same three moves work for the next fraction. The first two lines are given, and the last is yours.

workedSteps.text: Putting x = 7 in gives 0 ÷ 0, so simplify first.
The top is a difference of squares.
Cancel x − 7 for the inputs near 7, then let x approach 7 in what remains.

steps.headline: The limit does not depend on the value at the point

lead.text: So far the point of interest has been a gap, but the value there can be anything at all without disturbing the limit. Take f(x) = x + 4 for every x except 2, and suppose that someone then sets f(2) = 0, so that one dot sits far below the line. Or suppose f(2) is left undefined, as in the earlier fractions, or is set to 6, which puts the dot back on the line. In all three cases the *nearby* outputs are the same, and so is the limit.

afterFigure.text: A limit follows the **neighbours of the point and not the point itself**. It is a statement about the approach, which is why one displaced value, or one missing value, leaves it unchanged. When the value at the point does match the limit the graph has no break there, and that is the property the next lesson names.

blocks.text: The fraction (x² − 4)/(x − 2) is simple to evaluate at almost every input. At x = 3 it gives 5 ÷ 1, which is 5, and at x = 2.5 it gives 2.25 ÷ 0.5, which is 4.5. At x = 2 itself it cannot be evaluated at all, because the top and the bottom are both zero there and 0 ÷ 0 is not a number, so the graph of the fraction has a single missing point.

Whether such a gap can be given a meaning is the first question of calculus, and it is not an idle one. The slope of a curve at a single point, which this part of the course builds towards, turns out to be a fraction of exactly this kind, with zero on top and zero below at the *very* point where we want it. The figure shows the graph, with the two inputs that do work marked as dots and the input that does not marked as an open circle.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read where a function's outputs are heading from a table of nearby values, find that value by cancelling a common factor, and see why the value at the point itself plays no part.

recap.keyIdea: A limit is the value a function's outputs approach as the input approaches a point, and it does not depend on the function's value at that point.

blocks.text: The **limit** of a function as x approaches a point is the number its outputs head for when x gets close from either side. It ignores whatever the function does at the point itself, which may be undefined or may have been set to something else.

When direct substitution gives 0 ÷ 0, the fraction is *indeterminate* at that point and can usually be rewritten: factor the top, cancel the common factor, and let x approach the point in the expression that remains.

recap.nextHook: A graph can head for different values from its two sides, and the next lesson asks what that does to the function's continuity.

lessons.title: Both sides of a point

steps.headline: A limit can be taken from one side only, and the two sides need not agree

lead.text: A car park charges £1.50 for a stay of less than one hour and £4.50 for a stay of one hour or more, so the charge, as a function of the length of stay, breaks at the one-hour mark. Let the stay creep up towards one hour from *below*, at 50 minutes, then 55, then 59, and the charge is £1.50 every time. Let it come down towards one hour from *above*, at 70 minutes, then 65, then 61, and the charge is £4.50 every time.

Each of these is a [[limit|The value the outputs approach as the input approaches a point. Met in 'Approaching a value'.]] taken from one side only. The value the outputs approach as the input rises towards a point is the **left-hand limit**, marked with a small minus sign after the point, and the value they approach as the input falls towards it is the **right-hand limit**, marked with a plus sign. Writing c(t) for the charge in pounds after t hours, the two limits at one hour are:

afterFigure.text: The charge at exactly one hour is £4.50, which matches the right-hand limit and not the left. The value at the point belongs to one side or the other, or to neither, and it is **the one-sided limits that say what each side is doing** as it arrives.

lead.text: The simplest functions with a break take one value on one side and a different value on the other. Read the left side of this one, and remember that only the inputs below the point count.
When the two sides follow different formulas, each one-sided limit comes from the formula for that side. Decide which rule governs the inputs just above 1, and put 1 into it.

steps.headline: A limit exists at a point only when both sides lead to the same number

lead.text: For the car park the one-sided limits at one hour are £1.50 and £4.50, and no single number is approached as the stay nears an hour, because coming from below gives one answer and coming from above gives another. The **two-sided limit** at a point, which is what the word limit has meant until now, exists only when the [[left-hand limit|The value the outputs approach as the input rises towards the point. Met in 'Both sides of a point'.]] and the [[right-hand limit|The value the outputs approach as the input falls towards the point. Met in 'Both sides of a point'.]] both exist and are *equal*, and it then has their common value.

afterFigure.text: This is what happened with (x² − 4)/(x − 2) at 2, where the outputs approached 4 from both sides, and it is why that limit could be stated without qualification. In the first graph the outputs arrive at 1 from the left and at −2 from the right, so there is no two-sided limit; in the second both sides arrive at 3, and the limit is 3. When the sides disagree, **neither one of them nor their average can stand in for the limit**, because the outputs are not heading for any of those numbers from both directions.

lead.text: A function made of two pieces has a two-sided limit at the join only if both pieces lead to the same number there. Find what each piece approaches, and compare.

steps.headline: A function is continuous at a point when its value there equals its limit

lead.text: Some graphs can be drawn through a point without lifting the pen, and others cannot, and the figure shows four cases at x = 3. The first heads for 4 and has the value 4. The second heads for 4 but has no value at 3, the third jumps from one height to another, and in the fourth both sides head for 4 while the value at 3 is 2, so the dot sits off the line.

Each failure breaks a different one of three requirements. A function is **continuous** at a point when the function has a value there, when it has a [[two-sided limit|The number the outputs approach from both sides, when the two sides agree. Met in 'Both sides of a point'.]] there, and when the two are the *same number*. The pen-lifting picture is a useful guide, but the three requirements are what can be checked with arithmetic.

afterFigure.text: Continuity was made precise in the early nineteenth century, by Bernard Bolzano in 1817 and by Augustin-Louis Cauchy in 1821, each of whom described it by saying that a very small change in the input produces a very small change in the output.

steps.headline: Is f continuous at 2, when f(x) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2 and f(2) = 7?

lead.text: Test the **three requirements** in turn, and stop at the *first* that fails. The function is given by one rule away from 2 and by a separately assigned value at 2.

workedSteps.text: First requirement: does the function have a value at 2? It does, because 7 has been assigned.
Second requirement: does it have a limit at 2? Away from 2 the rule is x + 2, and the limit looks only at those inputs.
Third requirement: compare the value with the limit.
The first two requirements hold and the third fails, so f is not continuous at 2. The value 7 sits above the line that the nearby outputs follow.

lead.text: The same three requirements decide the next case, which is described in words and not drawn.

steps.headline: A missing or misplaced value can be repaired when the limit exists

lead.text: Suppose f(x) = 3x + 1 for every x except 2, where nothing has been assigned. Near 2 the outputs approach 3 × 2 + 1, which is 7, from both sides, so the limit exists and the only thing missing is a value to match it. Setting f(2) = 7 closes the gap, and the completed function is continuous at 2. A break of this kind is called **removable**, because a single assigned value removes it.

A jump cannot be mended in that way. If the left-hand limit is 1 and the right-hand limit is 6, any single value assigned at the point can match at most one of them, and the other side still arrives somewhere else.

afterFigure.text: The same repair applies when a value is present but wrong, as in the fourth graph of the last figure: the number to assign is always *the limit*. That makes **finding the limit the first task** whenever a function is to be made continuous.

lead.text: The repair is the same for any rule: find what the surrounding rule approaches, and assign exactly that.

lessons.orientation: Use the limits from each side of a point, and the value at the point, to decide whether a function is continuous there.

blocks.text: Consider a delivery fee that depends on the basket total: £3 for every total below £20, and £7 for £20 or more. The function has a value at every total, and yet its graph breaks at £20, because a basket of £19.99 costs £3 to deliver while a basket of £20.00 costs £7.

A break of this kind differs from the missing point of the last lesson. There the outputs agreed on a destination from both sides and only the point itself was in doubt; here the outputs on the left of £20 stay at one level and those on the right stay at another, so there is no single number to give in answer to the question of where the fee is heading. Telling these breaks apart, and saying exactly when a graph has no break at all, is the work of this lesson.

recap.keyIdea: A limit exists at a point when both sides lead to the same number, and a function is continuous there when its value also equals that limit.

blocks.text: A **left-hand limit** and a **right-hand limit** follow the outputs from one side only, and the two-sided limit exists only when they are equal. A function is continuous at a point when it has a value there, a two-sided limit there, and the two are the *same number*.
When only the value is missing or misplaced, the break is removable, because assigning the limit as the value repairs it. A jump cannot be repaired in that way, because its two sides disagree.

lessons.title: From average rate to instant rate

steps.headline: An average rate is the change in the output divided by the change in the input

lead.text: A tank holds 20 litres two minutes after a tap is opened and 50 litres at five minutes. Between those readings the amount rose by 30 litres while the time rose by 3 minutes, so on average the tank filled at 30 ÷ 3, or 10 litres every minute. This ratio of the change in the output, the *rise*, to the change in the input, the *run*, is called the **average rate** of change over the interval, and it equals the slope of the straight line that joins the two readings on a graph.
In symbols, for a function f between the inputs a and b, the average rate is:

afterFigure.text: An average describes the stretch as a whole. If the tap had run faster during the first minute and more slowly afterwards, the same two readings would give the same average, so **an average rate cannot say how fast anything was changing at one particular moment**.

lead.text: The odometer readings in the opening graph give an average rate in just this way. Work out the average speed of the car between the two readings.

reveal.text: Sixty kilometres in an hour and a half is the average over the whole stretch, and the car need not have been travelling at that speed at 2:00 or at any other moment. For the speed at 2:00 itself the stretch has to be made shorter, which is what the next screens do.

steps.headline: The average rate over an interval is the slope of the line through two points of the graph

lead.text: Take f(x) = x², whose graph is a parabola, and the interval from x = 0 to x = 2. The points on the graph are (0, 0) and (2, 4), and the line through them rises 4 over a run of 2, which is a slope of 2. The line through (0, 0) and (1, 1) has a slope of 1 instead, so the average rate depends on how long the interval is, even when the interval starts at the same place.

A straight line through two points of a curve is called a **secant**, from the Latin *secare*, to cut, because it cuts the curve at both points. Its slope is the [[average rate|The change in the output divided by the change in the input. Met earlier in this lesson.]] over the interval between them. In the figure, the slider shortens the interval from the right-hand end, so you can watch the secant turn as the second point moves in towards the first.

afterFigure.text: The secant changes as the interval changes, and it changes in a particular direction, towards a line that grips the curve at the starting point. The next screens put a number on that direction.

lead.text: A secant's slope needs only the heights at the two ends of the interval. Find them for x², subtract, and divide by the width of the interval.

steps.headline: As the interval shrinks, the secant slopes settle on one number

lead.text: Fix the start at x = 1 and let the interval run from 1 to 1 + h, where h is its length. For h = 1 the secant slope of x² is (4 − 1) ÷ 1, which is 3. For h = 0.5 it is (2.25 − 1) ÷ 0.5, which is 2.5, for h = 0.1 it is (1.21 − 1) ÷ 0.1, which is 2.1, and for h = 0.01 it is 2.01.

These slopes are heading for 2, so the secants are **settling into one line**, which touches the curve at x = 1. The same happens where the curve falls. Starting at x = −1, the intervals from −1 to −1 + h give slopes of −1, −1.5, −1.9 and −1.99, which head for −2, and the negative sign records that the curve is going *down* as x increases.

afterFigure.text: The slope of the secant is a fraction that depends on h, and the number the table is heading for is its [[limit|The value the outputs approach as the input approaches a point. Met in 'Approaching a value'.]] as h approaches 0. The figure shows the two starting points, and its slider shortens the interval.

steps.headline: The exact slope of x² at x = 1

lead.text: A table *suggests* the number, and **algebra settles it**. Here the secant slope from 1 to 1 + h is treated as a fraction in h, then simplified, then followed to its limit.

workedSteps.text: The secant slope is the change in the output over the change in the input, where f(x) = x². Putting h = 0 straight in would give 0 ÷ 0, an [[indeterminate form|0 ÷ 0, which does not settle a value. Met in 'Approaching a value'.]].
Expand the square, so that the 1 in the top cancels.
Because h is small but not zero, divide the top and the bottom by h.
Now let h approach 0. The 2 stays and the h vanishes, which agrees with the table.

steps.headline: The slope of x² at x = 2

lead.text: The same steps work at a new point. The first two lines are given, and the last is yours.

workedSteps.text: The secant from 2 to 2 + h has this slope.
Expand the square, subtract 4, and divide the top and the bottom by h, which is not zero.
Now let h approach 0 in what is left.

steps.headline: The limit of the secant slopes is the derivative, and it is the rate at that instant

lead.text: The number that the secant slopes settle on is called the **derivative** of the function at the point, and it is written f′(a) for the point x = a. As a formula, it is the [[limit|The value the outputs approach as the input approaches a point. Met in 'Approaching a value'.]] of the average rate over an interval that shrinks down to the point:

The line that the secants approach touches the curve at the point and does not cut through it nearby, and it is called the **tangent**, from the Latin *tangere*, to touch. The derivative is the slope of the tangent, and it is also the **instantaneous rate** of change, the rate at one moment, which an average over any stretch can only approximate. For f(x) = x² the algebra of the last two screens works at any point x, since ((x + h)² − x²) ÷ h simplifies to 2x + h, so the derivative is 2x. That gives 2 at x = 1 and 4 at x = 2, as before, and at x = −1 it gives −2, a tangent sloping downwards.

afterFigure.text: Gottfried Leibniz published the first account of the differential calculus in 1684, in the journal *Acta Eruditorum*. Isaac Newton had developed his own version in the 1660s but did not publish it until much later, and the quarrel between their followers over who deserved the credit lasted for years.

lead.text: The derivative at any point comes from the same shrinking secant. At x = 5 the algebra has been done as far as the fraction, and the limit is what is left.
The average rate of x² over the unit from 3 to 4 is 7, but an average over a stretch is not the rate at a moment. With the rule f′(x) = 2x, find the rate at the start of that stretch.

blocks.text: A car's odometer reads 40 km at 1:00 and 100 km at 2:30, and nobody looked at it at 2:00. Dividing the distance travelled by the time taken gives a speed for the whole stretch, but it cannot say how fast the car was going at 2:00 exactly, since the car may have been quicker at some moments and slower at others and the two readings are silent about which.

To ask about a single moment, the stretch has to be shortened around it, and that runs into the difficulty of the last two lessons: a stretch of no length covers no distance and takes no time, so the speed over it is 0 ÷ 0. The limit supplies the missing meaning, and what it gives is the central idea of calculus, a rate of change at a single instant.

recap.keyIdea: The slope of the secant over a shrinking interval settles on the derivative, which is the instantaneous rate of change at the point.

blocks.text: An **average rate** is the change in the output divided by the change in the input, and it is the slope of the secant through two points of the graph. Shrinking the interval and taking the limit of the secant slopes gives the **derivative** f′(a), which is the slope of the tangent and the instantaneous rate at that point.
For f(x) = x² the secant slope simplifies to 2x + h before h is allowed to approach 0, and so the derivative is 2x.

recap.nextHook: Finding each derivative from a limit is slow, and the next lesson gives a rule that does it for any power of x in one step.

lessons.title: A rule for powers

steps.headline: The derivative is itself a function: it gives a slope for every x

lead.text: For f(x) = x² the [[tangent|The line the secants approach; its slope is the derivative. Met in 'From average rate to instant rate'.]] at x = 1 has slope 2, and the tangent at x = 3 has slope 6. Each is a single number belonging to one point, but the rule that produced them, f′(x) = 2x, gives a slope for *every* x, and so the [[derivative|The limit of the secant slopes at a point: the slope of the tangent. Met in 'From average rate to instant rate'.]] is itself a function. The prime marks it as the derivative of f, and f′(3) = 6 is the value of that function at 3.

The two functions answer **different questions**, and mixing them up is a common slip. At x = 3 the function f gives the *height* of the curve, f(3) = 9, while the derivative f′ gives its *slope*, f′(3) = 6. In the figure, the height is where the tangent touches the curve and the slope is how steeply the tangent climbs.

afterFigure.text: Writing f′(x) once gives every slope at a stroke, which is far better than repeating the limit at each point. What remains is to write f′(x) quickly for other functions, and the slopes of x² already hold a clue.

lead.text: The slopes of x² at four points are listed in the question below. Look for the pattern in them and use it, without doing any algebra.

reveal.text: Each slope is twice its input: 2 × 1, 2 × 2, 2 × 3 and 2 × 5. The pattern is the derivative 2x, and it carries on without limit, so the slope at x = 7 is twice 7.

steps.headline: The power comes down in front, and the power drops by one

lead.text: The figure shows why the slope of x² is 2x. A square of side x has area x², and growing the side by h adds two strips of area xh and a small corner square of area h², so the area rises from x² to x² + 2xh + h². The gain is 2xh + h², and dividing it by the extra length h gives the [[secant slope|The slope of the line through two points of a curve. Met in 'From average rate to instant rate'.]] 2x + h, which becomes 2x as h shrinks.

A cube of side x grows in the same way, with three slabs of volume x²h, three bars of volume xh² and a corner cube h³, so the gain divided by h is 3x² + 3xh + h², and its limit is 3x². In general, expanding (x + h)ⁿ gives xⁿ, then a term in which one of the n brackets has supplied the h while the others supply x, and that term occurs n times, as nxⁿ⁻¹h; every other term contains h², and after dividing by h it still contains an h, which vanishes. This is the **power rule**, and to find a derivative by a rule of this kind is to **differentiate**:

afterFigure.text: The power comes down as a multiplier, and the power on x *drops* by one. Since x is x¹, **its derivative is 1 × x⁰, which is 1**, matching the fact that the line y = x has a slope of 1 everywhere.

lead.text: The power rule gives the whole derivative at once. The only care needed afterwards is to put the number into **the derivative** and *not* into the original function.

workedSteps.text: Bring the power down in front and lower the power by one.
Put x = 3 into the derivative, where 3³ is 27.
The height of the curve at 3 is a different number, because the function and its derivative answer different questions.

lead.text: Apply the rule to a cube, and then put the point into the result.

steps.headline: A constant multiplies through, and a constant added changes nothing

lead.text: Two further facts let the [[power rule|The derivative of xⁿ is n xⁿ⁻¹: the power comes down and drops by one. Met earlier in this lesson.]] cover every polynomial. If a function is multiplied by a constant, its derivative is multiplied by the same constant, so the derivative of 5x³ is 5 × 3x², which is 15x²; this is the **constant multiple rule**. And when functions are added, their derivatives are added, so to differentiate x³ + 4x you differentiate each term and obtain 3x² + 4, where the 4 comes from 4 × 1; this is the **sum rule**.

Adding a constant is the simplest case of all. Raising a whole graph by 3 moves every point up and leaves its *steepness* where it was, so the tangents keep their slopes and the derivative of a constant is 0. The figure shows the tangent at x = 1 for x² and for x² + 3, and its slope is the same, 2, in both.

afterFigure.text: Together the three rules differentiate a polynomial one term at a time: bring each power down, multiply by its coefficient, and discard any constant term.

steps.headline: Differentiating 2x² + 5 and evaluating at x = 1

lead.text: The multiple stays in front while the power rule acts on x², and the constant drops out. The first two lines are given, and the last is yours.

workedSteps.text: The multiple 2 stays, and the power rule makes the derivative of x² into 2x.
The constant 5 has slope 0, so it contributes nothing to the derivative.
Put x = 1 into the derivative.

lead.text: Combining the rules on a polynomial gives another polynomial. Differentiate each term in turn, and choose the expression that results.

steps.headline: The sign of the derivative says whether the curve is rising, flat or falling

lead.text: Because the derivative is a slope, **its sign carries information**. Take f(x) = x² + 4x, whose derivative is 2x + 4. For x less than −2, the derivative is negative and the curve is *falling*; at x = −2 it is zero and the tangent is *flat*; and for x greater than −2 it is positive and the curve is *rising*. The figure shows the tangent at x = −3, where the slope is −2, and at x = −2, where it is flat.

afterFigure.text: A flat tangent marks a place where the curve stops falling and starts to rise, here the bottom of a dip, and finding such places is one of the main uses of the derivative. Both signs and zeros of f′ are read directly from its formula, which is why a formula for the derivative is worth having.

lead.text: A minus sign in front of the squared term turns the parabola upside down. Apply the rules, and check that the sign of your answer fits a curve that is falling at that point.

blocks.text: The last lesson found that the slope of f(x) = x² at the point x is 2x, and getting there took a fraction, an expansion and a limit. Repeating that work for x³, x⁴ and x⁵ would be possible but slow, because the expansion grows with the power: (x + h)⁵ alone has six terms. There is a shortcut, and it comes from noticing what the answers look like.

A power of x has a slope at every point, and the shortcut writes that slope for any power at once. It has three parts, one for powers, one for constants and multiples, and one for sums, and together they give the derivative of any polynomial in a single line.

intro.promise: By the end you'll differentiate any polynomial term by term, tell a slope from a height, and use the sign of the derivative to say whether a curve is rising or falling.

recap.keyIdea: The derivative of xⁿ is nxⁿ⁻¹, and constants and sums pass through it, so any polynomial can be differentiated one term at a time.

blocks.text: The **power rule** says that the derivative of xⁿ is nxⁿ⁻¹, and the constant multiple rule and the sum rule let you differentiate a polynomial term by term, with any constant term contributing 0. The derivative f′ is a function in its own right: f′(a) is the *slope* at a, which is a different number from the height f(a).
Its sign shows the direction of the curve, negative where it falls, zero where the tangent is flat and positive where it rises.

lessons.title: A function inside a function

steps.headline: When one quantity depends on a second that depends on a third, the rates multiply

lead.text: A wage of £15 an hour, with the pounds then exchanged at 1.2 euros to the pound, is a chain of two stages. The first stage turns hours into pounds at 15 pounds per hour, and the second turns pounds into euros at 1.2 euros per pound. One hour of work earns 15 pounds, and 15 pounds buys 15 × 1.2 euros, which is 18 euros, so the rate from hours to euros is 18 euros per hour.

Nothing about this wage or this exchange rate is special. In any chain of stages, **the rate for the whole chain is the product of the rates of its stages**, because the output of one stage is the input of the next and each stage *scales* whatever reaches it. That multiplication is the idea behind the rule this lesson builds.

afterFigure.text: Both stage rates here are constants. When a stage is a curve, its rate changes from point to point, so the rate has to be taken at the right place: the second stage's rate is read at the value that the first stage has delivered.

lead.text: The bicycle in the opening figure is a chain of the same kind, with stage rates that you can multiply. Predict the result before working it through.

reveal.text: Three wheel turns per pedal turn and 2 metres per wheel turn multiply to 6 metres per pedal turn, and with one pedal turn each second that is 6 metres every second. Written with their units, the wheel turns cancel: wheel turns per pedal turn times metres per wheel turn leaves metres per pedal turn.

steps.headline: The derivative of a composition is the outer rate at the inner value, times the inner rate

lead.text: The function f(x) = (4x + 5)² is a chain of two stages. The first stage turns x into 4x + 5 and is called the **inner function**; the second squares whatever it receives and is called the **outer function**. Writing u for the output of the inner stage, u = 4x + 5 and f = u². Each stage has a rate: u changes by 4 for every unit of x, and by the [[power rule|The derivative of xⁿ is n xⁿ⁻¹. Met in 'A rule for powers'.]] f changes by 2u for every unit of u.

The rates *multiply*, with the outer rate taken *at the value that the inner stage delivers*, so the derivative is 2u × 4, which is 2(4x + 5) × 4, or 8(4x + 5). This is the **chain rule**: differentiate the outer function, keep the inner function inside it, and multiply by the derivative of the inner function. Expanding gives a check, since (4x + 5)² = 16x² + 40x + 25, whose derivative 32x + 40 is exactly 8(4x + 5). In Leibniz's notation, where df/du means the rate of f with respect to u, the rule reads:

afterFigure.text: The du seems to cancel, which is a handy reminder of the rule but not a proof of it. Without the factor 4 the answer would be 2(4x + 5), and at x = 0 that is 10, whereas the figure shows that the tangent of (4x + 5)² at 0 has slope 40. The curve (x + 5)² has an inner rate of 1, so for it the extra factor changes nothing, and its slope at 0 is 10.

steps.headline: The slope of (4x − 3)² at x = 2

lead.text: **Name** the inner and outer functions first, then differentiate the outside, then multiply by *the rate of the inside*.

workedSteps.text: The inner function is 4x − 3 and the outer function squares it.
Differentiate the outer function and keep the inner function inside it.
Multiply by the derivative of the inner function, which is 4.
Put in x = 2. The inner function has the value 5 there.

lead.text: In (2x + 1)² the inner function changes by 2 for every unit of x, so the chain rule brings in a factor of 2. Find the slope at x = 1.

steps.headline: When the inner function falls, its negative rate flips the sign

lead.text: An inner rate can be negative. In (4 − x)² the inner function 4 − x falls by 1 for each unit of x, so **its derivative is −1**, and the [[chain rule|Differentiate the outer function, keep the inner function inside it, and multiply by the derivative of the inner function. Met in 'A function inside a function'.]] gives 2(4 − x) × (−1), which is −2(4 − x). The curve is the same as (x − 4)², whose derivative is 2(x − 4), and the two expressions are equal, which confirms the sign.

The sign tells you the direction. At x = 1 the slope is −2 × 3, which is −6, because the curve is *falling* towards its lowest point at x = 4, and at x = 5 it is −2 × (−1), which is 2, because the curve is *rising* on the far side. **The inner rate decides the sign** of the factor, and the outer rate and the position decide the rest.

steps.headline: The slope of (3 − x)² at x = 1

lead.text: The inner function now falls, so its rate is negative. The first two lines are given, and the last is yours.

workedSteps.text: The inner function is 3 − x, which falls by 1 for each unit of x, and the outer function squares it.
The outer derivative at the inner value, times the inner rate.
Put x = 1 into the derivative.

lead.text: Chain-rule answers keep the inner function inside the outer derivative. Choose the expression that does, with the inner rate in place.

steps.headline: The same rule reads naturally for quantities that change in time

lead.text: A square patch of mould has a side of s centimetres, and the side grows at 2 centimetres a day. Its area is A = s², so each extra centimetre of side adds 2s square centimetres of area. When the side is 10 centimetres the area grows by 20 square centimetres for each centimetre of side, and the side is growing by 2 centimetres a day, so **the area grows at 20 × 2**, which is 40 square centimetres a day.

This is the [[chain rule|Differentiate the outer function, keep the inner function inside it, and multiply by the derivative of the inner function. Met earlier in this lesson.]] written in Leibniz's notation, with time at the start of the chain: **dA/dt = dA/ds × ds/dt**, where dA/ds is the rate of the area with respect to the side and ds/dt is the rate of the side with respect to time. Chains of this kind are everywhere in science, because a quantity of interest usually depends on something that is *itself* changing.

blocks.text: Pedalling a bicycle moves it in two stages. The pedals turn the wheel through the gearing, and the wheel carries the bicycle along the road, so how fast the bicycle moves depends on how many wheel turns each pedal turn produces and on how far each wheel turn carries it. Neither rate alone gives the speed, which is built from both.

Calculus meets the same structure whenever one quantity depends on a second that depends on a third, as in (2x + 1)². The square acts on a bracket, and the bracket changes as x does. The power rule of the last lesson handles x² on its own, but it cannot handle the bracket, and the rule for combining the two rates is the subject of this lesson.
