lessons.title: Read motion from a curve

steps.headline: Velocity is the rate at which position changes

lead.text: Position is a function of time, written s(t), and the average rate of change of s over an interval is the *average velocity*: the change in position divided by the change in time. For s(t) = 4t² the average velocity over the second second is (16 − 4) ÷ 1, which is 12 metres per second, and over the third second it is (36 − 16) ÷ 1, which is 20.

Shrinking the interval to a single moment turns the average into the [[derivative|The limit of the secant slopes at a point: the slope of the tangent. Met in 'From average rate to instant rate'.]], exactly as in the lesson on average rates, and the derivative of position is **velocity**: v(t) = s′(t). Its unit is the unit of the output per unit of the input, here metres per second, written m/s. Its sign carries a direction as well, because a positive velocity means that position is increasing and a negative velocity means that it is decreasing.
A lift rising steadily is the simplest case, since its position graph is a straight line and the slope is the same everywhere.

steps.headline: The power rule turns a position into a velocity at once

lead.text: For s(t) = 4t² the power rule gives v(t) = 8t, since the multiple 4 stays and the derivative of t² is 2t. At t = 1 second the velocity is 8 m/s, and at t = 3 seconds it is 24 m/s, which are the slopes of the [[tangents|The lines the secants approach; their slopes are derivatives. Met in 'From average rate to instant rate'.]] in the figure. The values fit the averages found earlier: the average over the second second, 12 m/s, lies between the velocities of 8 m/s and 16 m/s at its two ends.
A velocity found in this way describes **one instant**. At t = 2 seconds the velocity is 16 m/s, which is *not* the same number as the 12 m/s average over the second before it.
Differentiate each term of the position, then put in the time. The 2t term contributes a velocity of its own.

steps.headline: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes

lead.text: The velocity 8t is itself a function of time, and it has a derivative, 8. The rate at which velocity changes is called **acceleration**; it is the derivative of the velocity, and therefore the derivative of the derivative of position, which is called the **second derivative** and written s″(t). Here a(t) = 8, so the velocity rises by 8 m/s during every second, and the unit of acceleration is metres per second per second, written m/s².

The figure shows the velocity line v = 8t with a tangent at one second and another at three seconds. The tangent is the line itself, because a straight line has the same slope everywhere, and so the acceleration is the same at both times.

afterFigure.text: A constant acceleration of this kind describes objects falling close to the ground. Galileo showed in the early 1600s, with balls rolling down slopes, that the distance an object falls grows as the square of the time, which in this language says that its acceleration is constant, and he set out the result in his *Two New Sciences* of 1638.

steps.headline: Velocity and acceleration from s(t) = 3t² − t

lead.text: Differentiate once for the **velocity** and again for the *acceleration*, writing the unit beside each result.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate the position with the power rule to get the velocity.
Differentiate the velocity to get the acceleration.
Put in a time to read the velocity. The acceleration needs no time, because it is the same at all of them.

steps.headline: Acceleration from s(t) = t³

lead.text: The same two differentiations apply to a cubic position. The first is given, and the second and the evaluation are yours.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate the position to get the velocity.
Differentiate the velocity, then put in the time.

steps.headline: A negative velocity means moving backwards, and speed is its size

lead.text: Take s(t) = t² − 8t, so that the [[velocity|The derivative of position. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is v(t) = 2t − 8. At t = 1 second the velocity is −6 m/s, and at t = 5 seconds it is +2 m/s. The negative sign at the earlier time means that position is decreasing, so the object is moving *backwards*, towards smaller values of s, and the positive sign later means that it has turned round. The turn happens at t = 4 seconds, where the velocity is zero and the object is momentarily at rest.

**Speed** is how fast the object moves without regard to direction, and it is the size of the velocity: 6 m/s at t = 1 and 2 m/s at t = 5. Velocity can be negative but speed cannot, and **a falling position graph does not mean that the object is slowing down**, since at t = 1 it is moving *faster* than at t = 5 although its position is falling.
A position that falls and then rises has a negative velocity at first. Take care with the sign when you put in the time.

steps.headline: An average velocity over a stretch is not the velocity at its end

lead.text: For s(t) = 2t² the average velocity from t = 1 to t = 3 is (18 − 2) ÷ 2, which is 8 m/s. The velocity at t = 3 itself is 4 × 3, which is 12 m/s. The two differ because the object keeps speeding up during the stretch, so the average is pulled down by the slower early part. The figure shows both: the secant across the whole stretch and the tangent at three seconds.

The two agree **only when the velocity is constant**. Otherwise the wording of a question decides which is wanted: how fast *over this stretch* asks for the average, and how fast *at this moment* asks for the derivative.
The average velocity of s(t) = t² from t = 1 to t = 3 is 4 m/s, but the next question is about a single moment, and a single moment needs the derivative.

lessons.orientation: Read velocity and acceleration from a position curve as its first and second derivatives, with units and signs.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Take s(t) = 4t², the distance in metres that an object has moved from its starting point after t seconds. After 1 second it has moved 4 metres, after 2 seconds 16 metres and after 3 seconds 36 metres, so it covers 12 metres during the second second and 20 metres during the third. The object is going faster as time passes, and the numbers alone show it.

A graph of position against time records more than where the object is. Its steepness at each moment is how fast the object is moving, and the rate at which that steepness changes is how quickly the object is speeding up or slowing down. Reading motion from the curve means reading its slope, and then the slope of its slope, and the derivative gives both.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find velocity and acceleration from a position, give them their units, and read direction and speed from the sign of the velocity.

recap.keyIdea: Velocity is the derivative of position and acceleration is the derivative of velocity, with the sign of the velocity giving direction and its size giving speed.

blocks.text: **Velocity** is the derivative of position, in metres per second, and **acceleration** is the derivative of velocity, which is the second derivative of position, in metres per second squared. A negative velocity means moving backwards, and speed is the size of the velocity.
An average over a stretch is the slope of a secant and a value at one moment is the slope of a tangent, and they agree only when the velocity is constant.

recap.nextHook: A velocity of zero marks a moment of turning, and the next lesson uses flat tangents to find where any curve turns.

lessons.title: Where does the curve turn?

steps.headline: At the top of a rise the slope is zero

lead.text: Take the height of a ball as h(t) = 4t − t² metres after t seconds. Its derivative, 4 − 2t, is the [[velocity|The derivative of position. Met in 'Read motion from a curve'.]], and it is positive until t = 2, zero at t = 2 and negative afterwards. In the figure the tangent climbs at t = 1 second with a slope of 2, lies flat at t = 2 seconds, and slopes down at t = 3 seconds with a slope of −2.

afterFigure.text: A point where the derivative is zero is called a **stationary point**, because the tangent is horizontal there and, for a moving object, the object is momentarily *at rest*. At t = 2 the ball is at its highest, since h(2) = 8 − 4 gives a height of 4 metres, and the ball's path shows why: before that moment the height is increasing and after it the height is decreasing, so the turn must happen where the slope is zero.

lead.text: A ball thrown harder reaches its top later. Find the moment at which its velocity is zero.

steps.headline: A local maximum is where the slope changes from positive to negative

lead.text: Not every stationary point is a peak, but the peaks are among them, and the sign of the derivative on *each side* tells them apart. A **local maximum** is a point whose height is at least as great as that of every point near it. Approaching one the curve rises, so the derivative is positive; leaving it the curve falls, so the derivative is negative; and at the point itself the derivative passes through zero. The ball's height 4t − t² follows this pattern, since its derivative 4 − 2t is positive before t = 2, zero at t = 2 and negative after.
Finding a local maximum therefore has two parts: **solve f′(x) = 0** for the stationary points, and then **check the sign of f′** just *before* and just *after* each one.

afterFigure.text: Pierre de Fermat noticed in the 1630s that near the top of a smooth curve the height hardly changes when you move a little to either side, and he turned that observation into a method for finding maxima and minima, years before Newton and Leibniz developed the derivative.

steps.headline: The peak of f(x) = 12x − 3x²

lead.text: **Differentiate**, set the derivative to zero, and then *test the sign* on each side before calling the point a peak.

workedSteps.text: Differentiate with the power rule.
Set the derivative to zero and solve for the stationary point.
Test one point on each side of x = 2: the derivative is positive on the left and negative on the right.
So x = 2 is a local maximum, and its height comes from the function itself, not from the derivative.

lead.text: The first step of every search for a turn is the same: find where the tangent is horizontal.

steps.headline: Check the slope on both sides, because a flat tangent can be a peak, a dip or neither

lead.text: Take f(x) = x² − 2x. Its derivative 2x − 2 is zero at x = 1. To the left of 1 the derivative is negative, as at x = 0 where it is −2, so the curve is falling; to the right it is positive, as at x = 2 where it is 2, so the curve is rising. A point where the curve falls and then rises is a **local minimum**, the mirror image of a local maximum.

afterFigure.text: Reading the signs of the derivative from left to right gives the rule: positive then negative marks a local maximum, negative then positive marks a local minimum, and the same sign on both sides marks *neither*, even though the tangent is flat. The last case does occur, and the next question looks at it.

lead.text: A flat tangent does not guarantee a turn. Look at the sign of the slope on each side of the flat point of x³, which is 3x².

steps.headline: On a closed interval, the highest and lowest values lie at a stationary point or at an end

lead.text: Often a question restricts x to a stretch of the curve, such as 0 ≤ x ≤ 5, which is written [0, 5] and called a **closed interval** because it includes both ends. A continuous function on a closed interval always has a highest and a lowest value there, called its **absolute maximum** and **absolute minimum**, and for a smooth function such as a polynomial each is found either at a [[stationary point|A point where the derivative is zero and the tangent is horizontal. Met in 'Where does the curve turn?'.]] inside the interval or at one of the two ends. The ends have to be checked *separately*, because the derivative need not be zero there: the curve may simply be cut off while it is *still* climbing.

Take f(x) = x² − 4x on [0, 5]. Its derivative 2x − 4 is zero at x = 2, where f(2) = −4. The ends give f(0) = 0 and f(5) = 5. The largest of the three values, 5, is the absolute maximum, and it occurs at the right-hand end, where the tangent is far from flat, as the figure shows; the smallest, −4, is the absolute minimum.

afterFigure.text: The method therefore has three steps: find the stationary points inside the interval, work out the function at each of them and at both ends, and compare the values.

lead.text: A straight line has no stationary point, so on an interval only the two ends can supply its highest and lowest values.
Here the stationary point is inside the interval, but it is the lowest value and not the highest, so the answer lies at an end.

lessons.orientation: Find where a curve turns by setting its derivative to zero, classify each turn by the sign of the slope on either side, and check the ends of an interval.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The velocity of a ball thrown upwards is positive on the way up and negative on the way down, so at the top, where it changes from one to the other, it must pass through zero. That observation turns the problem of finding the highest point into the problem of finding where a derivative is zero, and it works for any smooth curve and not only for the path of a ball.

Curves that peak, dip or level off are common in applications, from the best price to the least material for a container, and finding a highest or lowest value is among the main uses of the derivative. This lesson shows how to find the places where a curve turns, how to tell a peak from a dip and from a mere pause, and why the ends of an interval must be checked as well.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find where a curve's tangent is flat, say whether the point is a maximum, a minimum or neither, and find the greatest or least value on an interval.

recap.keyIdea: A curve can turn only where its derivative is zero, the signs of the derivative on either side say what kind of turn it is, and on an interval the ends must be checked too.

blocks.text: A **stationary point** is where the derivative is zero. It is a local maximum if the slope changes from positive to negative, a local minimum if it changes from negative to positive, and neither if the sign stays the same.
On a closed interval the absolute maximum and minimum are found by comparing the values at the stationary points inside the interval with the values at both ends.

recap.nextHook: Differentiation turns a curve into its slope, and the next lesson runs that process backwards, recovering a function from its derivative.

lessons.title: Undo a rate of change

steps.headline: A rate can be run backwards to recover the quantity that produced it

lead.text: Differentiation turns a quantity into its rate: the derivative of the position t² is the velocity 2t, and the derivative of t³ is 3t². Read in the other direction, these facts answer a question that arises just as often. A speedometer reports a rate, and so does a flow meter, but the quantity wanted is usually the total, the distance covered or the volume that has flowed, and **the total is a function whose derivative is the rate**.

When the rate is constant, recovering the total is multiplication: 4 litres per minute for 3 minutes is 12 litres. When the rate changes, the total has to be found by undoing the differentiation, and for powers of x that can often be done by inspection. The velocity 2t is the derivative of t², so t² is a candidate for the position, and *checking* is easy, because differentiating a candidate must return the rate we started from.

steps.headline: Many functions have the same derivative, and they differ by a constant

lead.text: There is a catch in running the power rule backwards. The rate 6x is the derivative of 3x², but it is also the derivative of 3x² + 3 and of 3x² − 7, because a constant added to a function does not change its slope, a fact met as the [[derivative of a constant|The derivative of a constant is 0, because raising a graph leaves its slopes unchanged. Met in 'A rule for powers'.]]. Every function whose derivative is 6x is called an **antiderivative** of 6x, and there are *infinitely many* of them, one for each constant.

The figure shows two of them. Their curves have the same shape, one lifted 3 units above the other, so their tangents are parallel at every x and the rate 6x is the same for both. All the antiderivatives of 6x are therefore written together as 3x² + C, where C stands for an arbitrary constant.
The family of antiderivatives is described by one expression with a constant in it. Choose the description that is complete and correct.

steps.headline: A known value fixes the constant

lead.text: The constant C is the one piece of information that the rate cannot supply, because a rate says how a quantity changes and not where it started. A single known value of the function supplies it. Suppose F′(x) = 6x and F(1) = 5. Every antiderivative has the form F(x) = 3x² + C, and putting x = 1 gives 3 + C, which must equal 5, so C = 2 and F(x) = 3x² + 2. **Exactly one member of the family** passes through the point (1, 5).
A value of this kind is called an *initial value* when it is given at the start, such as the position at time 0, and it turns the family of antiderivatives into a single function.
With the starting value at x = 0, the polynomial part of the antiderivative vanishes, and the constant can be read off directly.

steps.headline: Raise the power by one and divide by the new power

lead.text: Differentiating xⁿ⁺¹ brings down the factor n + 1, so undoing it means *dividing* by n + 1. That reverses the [[power rule|The derivative of xⁿ is n xⁿ⁻¹: the power comes down and drops by one. Met in 'A rule for powers'.]]: **an antiderivative of xⁿ is xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1)**, plus a constant, for any n except −1. For example, an antiderivative of 5x⁴ is x⁵, and an antiderivative of 6x² is 2x³, since 6 ÷ 3 is 2. Constants and sums pass through as they did for derivatives, so an antiderivative of 4x + 3 is 2x² + 3x, where 4x gives 2x² and the constant 3 gives 3x.

The whole family is called the **indefinite integral**, and it is written with a long S and a dx, as in ∫ 4x dx = 2x² + C. Leibniz introduced the sign in 1675, as a stretched S for the Latin *summa*, a sum, which hints at the second half of this course.

steps.headline: Recovering F from F′(x) = 12x² and F(0) = 5

lead.text: **Undo** the differentiation first, with a constant in the answer, and then use the known value to *find the constant*.

workedSteps.text: Undo the power: raise the power of x by one and divide by the new power.
Use the known value to fix the constant: at x = 0 the term 4x³ vanishes.
The function is now fully determined, and its value anywhere can be read off.

steps.headline: Recovering F from F′(x) = 3x² and F(0) = 0

lead.text: The same two moves apply to the next rate. The first two lines are given, and the last is yours.

workedSteps.text: Undo the power, dividing by the new power.
At x = 0 the term x³ vanishes, so the starting value of 0 fixes the constant.
Put x = 2 into the function.

lead.text: Rates of motion pose the same problem in context. The velocity gives the position up to a constant, and the position at the start fixes the constant.
A rate with two terms is undone term by term, and the constant is fixed at the end.

lessons.orientation: Run differentiation backwards to recover a function from its rate, using a known value to fix the constant.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Differentiating x² gives 2x, and so does differentiating x² + 5 or x² − 100, because a constant added to a function does not change its slope. Going the other way, from 2x back to a function that has it as its derivative, therefore has no single answer, and this lesson is about handling that honestly.

Running differentiation backwards matters because rates are often known before totals. A speedometer reports a rate, and the distance covered is the quantity wanted. The method undoes the power rule, and it needs one extra piece of information, a starting value, to settle which of the many possible answers is the one that is needed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll undo the power rule to find a function from its rate, write the whole family of answers, and use a starting value to choose one.

recap.keyIdea: A function is recovered from its rate by undoing the power rule and adding a constant, and one known value of the function fixes that constant.

blocks.text: An **antiderivative** of a rate is a function whose derivative it is, and all the antiderivatives of a rate differ by a constant. Undoing the power rule raises the power by one and divides by the new power, and one known value fixes the constant.
The family of all antiderivatives is the indefinite integral, so ∫ 4x dx = 2x² + C.

recap.nextHook: So far the antiderivative has been found by undoing powers; the next lesson builds the same quantity from thin strips of area.

lessons.title: Build an area from strips

steps.headline: When the rate is constant, the amount is the area of a rectangle

lead.text: When a rate is constant, **the amount that accumulates is the rate multiplied by the time**. A tank filled at 3 litres per minute for 4 minutes receives 3 × 4 = 12 litres, and on a graph of rate against time the same product is the area of a rectangle, 3 high and 4 wide. The area under the graph is the amount, and the units agree: litres per minute multiplied by minutes leaves litres.

Nothing here depends on water. A velocity in metres per second held for some seconds gives metres, and a price in pounds per kilogram multiplied by a mass in kilograms gives pounds, so the area under *any* graph of a rate carries the units of the rate multiplied by the units of its input.
A rate that changes in steps is handled one stretch at a time: find the amount for each stretch, then add.

steps.headline: When the rate keeps changing, add up many thin rectangles

lead.text: Now let the rate change. Suppose it is 2x litres per minute at x minutes after the tap is opened, so the tank fills slowly at first and faster later. No single rate multiplies the three minutes, but over a short stretch the rate *hardly* changes, and a short stretch can be treated as though the rate were constant. Cut the interval from 0 to 3 into three strips of width 1, and on each strip use the rate at its left edge, which is 0, 2 and 4 litres per minute. The three amounts are 0 × 1, 2 × 1 and 4 × 1, and they add up to 6 litres.

Each product is the area of a rectangle, and the total of the areas is called a **rectangle sum**. A rectangle whose height is the function's value at the left edge of its strip is a **left-endpoint rectangle**. With six strips of width 0.5 the left-edge heights are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, and the sum is 15 × 0.5, or 7.5 litres. The figure shows both.

afterFigure.text: The sums are climbing, from 6 to 7.5. The graph of 2x is a straight line, so the true area under it from 0 to 3 is a triangle with a base of 3 and a height of 6, which is ½ × 3 × 6, or 9. The left rectangles all sit below the line because the rate is rising, so each of these sums falls short of 9, and thinner strips close the gap.

steps.headline: Three left-endpoint rectangles for f(x) = x on [0, 3]

lead.text: Find the **width** of a strip, read the heights at the *left edges*, and add the areas.

workedSteps.text: Three equal strips across an interval of length 3 each have a width of 1.
The left edges are 0, 1 and 2, and the heights are the values of f there.
Add the three areas, each a height times the width of 1. The true area under the line is the triangle ½ × 3 × 3, or 4.5, so the sum falls short, as it should for a rising function.

lead.text: Two strips are wider, and the sum is coarser. Find the width of each strip, then read the heights at the left edges.

steps.headline: Using the right edge instead gives an overestimate when the rate rises

lead.text: Each strip can equally take its height from its right edge. For the same three strips of 2x, the right-edge heights are 2, 4 and 6, and the sum is 2 + 4 + 6, or 12. A rectangle of this kind is a **right-endpoint rectangle**. Its top lies above the line, because the rate is *still* climbing at the right edge of the strip, and so the sum overshoots.

afterFigure.text: For a rising rate the true amount is trapped between the two sums: the left sum of 6 is too small, the right sum of 12 is too big, and the true value of 9 lies between them. For a falling rate the order would reverse. The gap between the two sums depends on the width of the strips, and the next screen makes the strips thinner.

steps.headline: Four right-endpoint rectangles for f(x) = x on [0, 4]

lead.text: The same steps apply with right edges. The first two lines are given, and the last is yours.

workedSteps.text: Four equal strips across an interval of length 4 each have a width of 1.
The right edges are 1, 2, 3 and 4, and the heights are the values of f there.
Multiply each height by the width and add.

steps.headline: Thinner strips close in on the exact amount, and the number they approach is the definite integral

lead.text: With six strips of width 0.5 the left edges give 7.5 and the right edges give 10.5, which bracket 9 more tightly than the three-strip sums of 6 and 12. A third choice takes each height from the middle of its strip. The heights at 0.25, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25 and 2.75 are 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5 and 5.5, which add to 18, and 18 × 0.5 is 9. This is the **midpoint rectangle**: it lies above the line on one half of its strip and below it on the other, and for a straight line the two errors cancel *exactly*.

In general the [[rectangle sums|The total area of the rectangles. Met earlier in this lesson.]] come closer to the true amount as the strips narrow, and the number they approach as the number of strips grows without limit is the **definite integral** of the function over the interval. It is written with the long S of the last lesson, which can now be read for what it is, a stretched S for a sum:

Unlike the [[indefinite integral|The family of all antiderivatives of a rate, written with the long S. Met in 'Undo a rate of change'.]], which is a family of functions, the definite integral is **a single number**.

afterFigure.text: Cauchy defined the integral of a continuous function as the limit of sums of this kind in 1823, and Bernhard Riemann widened the definition in a paper of 1854, which is why such sums are often called Riemann sums.

lead.text: The two sums for a rising rate were on opposite sides of the true amount. Decide on which side the left-endpoint sum always lies.
A midpoint rectangle reads the function in the middle of its strip. Find the width and the midpoints first.

lessons.orientation: Estimate an accumulated amount by adding rectangles under a rate graph, and see how thinner strips lead to the definite integral.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Suppose the rate at which a tank fills is 2x litres per minute at x minutes after the tap is opened, so that it fills slowly at first and faster as time passes. How much water enters in the first three minutes? Multiplication does not answer it, because there is no single rate to multiply by the three minutes.

The idea that does answer it is to cut the interval into short strips, treat the rate as constant on each strip, and add up what each strip contributes. The sums that result are areas of rectangles, they can be made as accurate as we like, and the number they approach is the second great idea of calculus, the integral.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate an accumulated amount with left, right and midpoint rectangles, and say what the rectangle sums approach as the strips get thinner.

recap.keyIdea: The area under a rate graph is the amount accumulated, and rectangle sums approach the definite integral as the strips get thinner.

blocks.text: Rate times time is the area of a rectangle, so for a changing rate the amount is estimated by cutting the interval into strips and adding rectangles whose heights are the rate at the left edge, the right edge or the middle of each strip. For a rising rate the left sum falls short of the true amount and the right sum overshoots it.
As the strips narrow, the sums close in on one number, the **definite integral**, which is a single number and not a family of functions.

recap.nextHook: A rate below zero takes amount away instead of adding it, and the next lesson gives areas a sign.

lessons.title: When areas cancel

steps.headline: Net change is the amount added minus the amount removed

lead.text: A rate below zero takes amount away. A tank filled at 5 litres per minute for 2 minutes gains 5 × 2 = 10 litres, and a tank drained at 3 litres per minute for 4 minutes changes by (−3) × 4 = −12 litres, because the rate is −3. On a graph of rate against time the first rectangle stands above the axis and the second hangs below it, and the sizes of their areas, 10 and 12, are the amounts moved.

The change that actually occurs is the amount added minus the amount removed, which is called the **net change**. The signs do the subtracting *automatically*: rectangles above the axis count as positive, rectangles below it count as negative, and the net change is their sum. A tank filled for 2 minutes at 5 and then drained for 4 minutes at 3 would end 10 − 12 = −2 litres lower than it began.
The draining stretch takes away from the filling stretch. Work out the change for each stretch with its sign, and add.

steps.headline: Where the graph runs below the axis, its area counts as negative

lead.text: Take the rate f(x) = x from x = −1 to x = 2. It is negative between −1 and 0 and positive between 0 and 2, so its graph is a line that crosses the axis, with a small triangle below it on the left and a larger triangle above it on the right. The small triangle has a base of 1 and a height of 1, so its size is ½ × 1 × 1, or 0.5, and the large one has a base of 2 and a height of 2, so its size is ½ × 2 × 2, or 2.

The rectangle sums of the last lesson multiply each width by the height of the function, so wherever the height is *negative* the product is negative, and the [[definite integral|The number the rectangle sums approach as the strips get thinner. Met in 'Build an area from strips'.]] inherits that sign. It is the **signed area**: the area above the axis counted positively, minus the area below the axis. Here it is −0.5 + 2, or 1.5, and the second case in the figure shows the left region alone, where the integral is −0.5.
A constant negative rate gives a rectangle that hangs below the axis. Its signed area is the rate multiplied by the width, with the sign kept.

steps.headline: The signed area of f(x) = x from −2 to 4

lead.text: The graph is a line through the origin, so the region between it and the axis is two triangles, one on each side of 0. Find the size of each, give the one below the axis **a minus sign**, and add.

workedSteps.text: On the left, from −2 to 0, the graph lies below the axis. The triangle has a base of 2 and a height of 2, and its signed area is negative.
On the right, from 0 to 4, the graph lies above the axis. The triangle has a base of 4 and a height of 4.
The signed area is the sum of the two, and the small negative part reduces the large positive one.

steps.headline: The signed area of f(x) = x from −2 to 2

lead.text: The two triangles are now mirror images of each other. The first two lines are given, and the last is yours.

workedSteps.text: On the left, the triangle has a base of 2 and a height of 2, and lies below the axis.
On the right, the triangle is the same size and lies above the axis.
Add the two signed areas.

steps.headline: Total area adds the sizes, while signed area keeps the signs

lead.text: Signed area answers the question of net change, but sometimes the quantity wanted is the total size of everything between the graph and the axis, such as the total distance travelled by an object that moves *forwards* and then *backwards*. This is the **total area**, and it **counts every region positively**. To find it, split the interval where the graph crosses the axis, find the size of each region, and add the sizes.

For f(x) = x on [−3, 1], the region below the axis is a triangle with a base of 3 and a height of 3, so its size is 4.5, and the region above is a triangle with a base of 1 and a height of 1, so its size is 0.5. The [[signed area|The area above the axis counted positive, minus the area below it. Met in 'When areas cancel'.]] is −4.5 + 0.5, or −4, while the total area is 4.5 + 0.5, or 5. The two numbers differ because they answer different questions, even though they come from the same graph, as they did for the object moving at 60 km/h forwards and then backwards.
The total area counts both triangles as positive. Find the size of each and add.

steps.headline: Swapping the bounds of an integral changes its sign

lead.text: An integral from a to b runs through the interval in the direction from a to b. Running it the other way, from b to a, reverses the direction of every strip, so the widths of the strips become negative while the heights *stay the same*, and each product changes sign. The **bounds** of an integral are its two ends, a and b, and swapping them changes the sign of the result:
For the constant rate 2, the integral from 0 to 4 is 2 × 4, or 8, and the integral from 4 back to 0 is −8. An integral between equal bounds is 0, since there are no strips at all.
Swap the bounds, and every strip is run through in the opposite direction.

lessons.orientation: Count area above the axis as positive and below it as negative, so that integrals give net change, and see how swapping the bounds changes the sign.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: An object whose velocity is +60 km/h for one hour and −60 km/h for the next ends where it began, although it has travelled 120 km. The area method of the last lesson gives 60 for the first hour and −60 for the second, and adding them gives 0, the change in position, while the 120 is the total distance. Both numbers are useful, and they come from the same graph by different arithmetic.

A graph that runs above the axis and then below it therefore needs a convention. The amount that has built up is not the area of everything between the graph and the axis, but a balance in which the parts above and below pull in opposite directions. Seeing how the balance is struck, and when the parts cancel, is the work of this lesson.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count area below the axis as negative, tell net change from total area, and know what happens to an integral when its bounds are swapped.

recap.keyIdea: A definite integral counts area above the axis as positive and below it as negative, so it gives net change, and swapping its bounds changes its sign.

blocks.text: The definite integral is a **signed area**: area above the axis counts as positive and area below it as negative, and the result is the net change in the quantity whose rate is graphed. The total area, which adds the sizes of the regions, answers a different question.
Swapping the bounds of an integral changes its sign, and an integral between equal bounds is 0.

recap.nextHook: A signed area is built from rectangles, which is slow; the next lesson shows that antiderivatives, from earlier in the course, compute it exactly.

lessons.title: Rates and areas connect

steps.headline: The area under 2x can be counted with triangles

lead.text: Take a tap whose flow rate after x minutes is r(x) = 2x litres per minute. Its graph is a straight line through the origin, so the area under it from the start to any later minute is **a triangle**. By the end of the first minute the rate has reached 2, and the triangle has a base of 1 and a height of 2, so its area is ½ × 1 × 2 = 1. By the end of the second minute the rate has reached 4, and the area is ½ × 2 × 4 = 4.

In the last two lessons an area under a rate graph was an amount, so each of these is the water that has flowed *so far*: 1 litre after one minute and 4 litres after two. The figure shows both triangles.
The same counting gives the amount that has flowed by the end of the third minute.

steps.headline: The running total of the area is an antiderivative of the rate

lead.text: Write A(x) for the area under 2x from 0 to x, the running total of the water. We have A(1) = 1, A(2) = 4 and A(3) = 9, which are 1², 2² and 3², and in general the triangle with a base of x and a height of 2x has area ½ × x × 2x = x². So **A(x) = x²**.

Now compare the *slope* of this running total with the *rate*. The derivative of x² is 2x, which is the rate r(x) itself. At minute 2 the total x² is growing at 4 litres per minute, the same number as the rate r(2) = 4. That is what a running total ought to do, since an amount grows exactly as fast as it is being added, and it means that the running total of the area is an [[antiderivative|A function whose derivative is the given rate. Met in 'Undo a rate of change'.]] of the rate.

cases.label: Slope of the total at minute 2

steps.headline: The area between two inputs is the difference of an antiderivative's values

lead.text: Because the running total from 0 is an antiderivative of the rate, **the amount added between two inputs a and b is the total up to b less the total up to a**. For 2x, with the [[antiderivative|A function whose derivative is the given rate. Met in 'Undo a rate of change'.]] x², the water that flows between minute 2 and minute 3 is 3² − 2² = 9 − 4 = 5 litres. The region is a trapezium with heights 4 and 6 and a width of 1, whose area is (4 + 6) ÷ 2 × 1 = 5, which agrees.

The same subtraction works for any rate that has an antiderivative. The statement is the **fundamental theorem of calculus**: if F is an antiderivative of a [[continuous|A function whose value at each point equals its limit there. Met in 'Both sides of a point'.]] function f, then the integral of f from a to b is F(b) − F(a). It is usually written with square brackets to show the two values being taken:

afterFigure.text: The theorem joins the two halves of the course, because an integral defined by adding thin rectangles can be computed by undoing a derivative. Isaac Barrow, who held the Lucasian chair at Cambridge before Newton, stated and proved a geometric form of it in his *Lectiones geometricae* of 1670, and Newton and Leibniz each turned it into a method.

steps.headline: The integral of 6x² from 1 to 2

lead.text: Find an **antiderivative** by undoing the power rule, evaluate it at the two bounds, and *subtract the lower value from the upper*.

workedSteps.text: An antiderivative of 6x² comes from raising the power and dividing by the new one, with no constant needed.
Evaluate the antiderivative at the upper bound and at the lower bound.
Subtract the lower value from the upper value.

steps.headline: The integral of 2x + 1 from 0 to 2

lead.text: A rate with two terms has an antiderivative with two terms. The first line is given, and the evaluation is yours.

workedSteps.text: Undo each term: 2x gives x², and the constant 1 gives x.
Evaluate the antiderivative at 2 and at 0, and subtract the lower value from the upper.

steps.headline: Any antiderivative will do, because the constant cancels

lead.text: An antiderivative is defined only up to a constant, so 2x has the antiderivatives x², x² + 7 and x² − 100. The theorem would be of little use if its answer depended on the choice, but it does *not*. Using F(x) + C, the integral from a to b is (F(b) + C) − (F(a) + C), and **the two constants subtract to nothing**. Using x² + 7 for the water between minute 2 and minute 3 gives (9 + 7) − (4 + 7), which is 5 as before. The simplest choice, C = 0, is always available, and it is the one to use.
Test the cancellation with an antiderivative that carries a large constant.

steps.headline: The rate at which an accumulated total grows is the rate being accumulated

lead.text: Fix a starting point and let the end point move. The [[integral|The definite integral: the number the rectangle sums approach. Met in 'Build an area from strips'.]] from 0 to x of the rate f(t), written with the letter t inside so that x can stay free as the end point, is the amount accumulated by x, and it is called an **accumulation function**, A(x). When x increases by a little, A gains a thin sliver of area whose height is about f(x), so A grows *at the rate f(x)*. That is the other half of the theorem: the derivative of the accumulation function is the rate that is being accumulated.
For f(t) = 2t the accumulation function is A(x) = x², and A′(x) = 2x = f(x), as the figure shows at minute 3: the total of 9 litres is growing at 6 litres per minute, the value of the rate there.

afterFigure.text: The two halves say that integrating and differentiating undo each other. Differentiate an accumulated total and the rate comes back, and evaluate the integral of a derivative and the change in the original function comes back.

cases.label: Slope of the total at minute 3

lead.text: An accumulated total grows at the rate being added, so the question needs no integration. Read the rate at the right moment.
The rate is now a quadratic with a constant term, and the answer is read off in the same way.

lessons.orientation: Evaluate definite integrals with antiderivatives, and see that differentiating an accumulated total returns the rate.

blocks.text: The derivative and the integral were built in different ways. One shrinks a secant to a tangent, and the other adds up thin rectangles, and nothing in either construction suggests that they have anything to do with each other. Yet the long S was used for both antiderivatives and areas in the last lessons, and that was no accident.

A test case shows why. The area under the rate 2x can be found with triangles, and an antiderivative of 2x can be found by undoing the power rule. If the two ideas are related, the two answers should be related as well, and the lesson follows that relation to the theorem that links the two halves of the course.

intro.promise: By the end you'll evaluate a definite integral by subtracting values of an antiderivative, say why the constant cancels, and find how fast an accumulated total is growing.

recap.keyIdea: The integral of a rate from a to b is F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F, and the derivative of an accumulation function is the rate it accumulates.

blocks.text: The **fundamental theorem of calculus** has two halves. The integral of a rate from a to b is F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F, because the constant cancels in the subtraction, and the derivative of the accumulation function from a fixed start up to x is the rate evaluated at x.
Integrating and differentiating therefore undo each other, which is why an area made of rectangles can be computed by reversing a derivative.

recap.nextHook: With net rates and starting values the theorem answers the practical question of how much a quantity has changed, which is the subject of the last lesson.

lessons.title: How much has changed?

steps.headline: At a steady rate, the change is the rate times the time

lead.text: A tap delivers 4 litres per minute, steadily. In 3 minutes it delivers 4 × 3 = 12 litres and in 6 minutes it delivers 4 × 6 = 24 litres, and on a graph of rate against time these are the areas of two rectangles of height 4. For a constant rate **the change is the rate multiplied by the time**, and the units combine as litres per minute times minutes, which leaves litres.

The amount delivered is only the change in the tank, however, and *not* what the tank holds. What it holds also depends on what it held to begin with, a point that this lesson returns to once the rate is allowed to vary.
The change is not the same as the amount present. Work out the change over the four minutes, and then decide what to do with the starting amount.

steps.headline: When the rate changes, the change in the amount is the integral of the rate

lead.text: If the inflow is 2t + 1 litres per minute at time t, no single rate multiplies the time, so the change in the amount over the first 3 minutes is the area under the graph of 2t + 1 from 0 to 3. The [[fundamental theorem|If F is an antiderivative of a continuous f, the integral of f from a to b is F(b) − F(a). Met in 'Rates and areas connect'.]] finds it from an antiderivative: t² + t has the derivative 2t + 1, so the change is (3² + 3) − (0² + 0) = 12 litres. The figure shows the region, a trapezium with heights 1 and 7 and a width of 3, whose area (1 + 7) ÷ 2 × 3 is also 12.

In general, **the change in any quantity from time a to time b is the integral of its rate of change** over that interval. This is the **net change theorem**, and it turns a rate, which is what instruments measure, into a change, which is what people *want to know*.

steps.headline: The water that enters at 3t² + 1 litres per minute between t = 1 and t = 2

lead.text: The change over an interval is the integral of the rate. Find an **antiderivative**, evaluate it at both ends, subtract, and then *read the unit*.

workedSteps.text: An antiderivative of the rate comes from undoing the power rule term by term.
Evaluate the antiderivative at the end and at the start of the interval.
Subtract the starting value from the end value. The result is an amount of water.

lead.text: Integrate the rate over the first two minutes, and keep the unit in mind.

steps.headline: The amount present is the starting amount plus the change

lead.text: The integral of a rate gives only the change in an amount, and **what a container holds also depends on what it held at the start**. If a tank holds 20 litres at t = 0 and the inflow is 2t + 1 litres per minute, then after 3 minutes it holds the starting 20 litres plus the 12 litres that came in, which is 32 litres. In symbols, the amount at time T is the starting amount plus the integral of the rate from 0 to T.

Forgetting the first term is the most common slip in problems of this kind, and checking the units does *not* catch it, because both terms are in litres. The check that does catch it is to put T = 0, when no time has passed and the amount must equal the starting amount.

steps.headline: A tank that starts with 7 litres and gains 2t + 3 litres per minute

lead.text: The change over the first two minutes comes first, and the starting amount is added to it. The first line is given, and the second is yours.

workedSteps.text: The change in the amount is the integral of the rate from 0 to 2.
Add the starting amount to the change to find what the tank holds at t = 2.

steps.headline: When water also leaves, integrate the net rate

lead.text: A tank may lose water as well as gain it, and then it is the **net rate** that matters, the inflow rate minus the outflow rate. Take an inflow of 2t litres per minute and an outflow of 3 litres per minute. The net rate is 2t − 3, which is negative until t = 1.5, while the outflow is the *larger* of the two and the amount falls, and positive afterwards. Over the first 2 minutes the inflow alone would add 4 litres, but the outflow removes 3 × 2 = 6, so the [[net change|The amount added minus the amount removed. Met in 'When areas cancel'.]] is 4 − 6 = −2 litres. Integrating the net rate gives the same number, since (t² − 3t) is 4 − 6 at t = 2 and 0 at t = 0.

afterFigure.text: The two routes always agree, because the integral of a difference is the difference of the integrals. Combining the rates first is usually shorter, and it keeps the signs in one place.

lead.text: Combine the two flows into one number, with the outflow counting against the inflow.

steps.headline: Displacement is the integral of velocity, while distance needs the sign changes split

lead.text: A car has the velocity v(t) = 4 − 2t metres per second, so it moves forwards until t = 2, when its velocity is zero, and backwards afterwards. The integral of velocity is its **displacement**, the change in position with the *direction* counted. From 0 to 3 seconds it is (4t − t²) evaluated from 0 to 3, which is 12 − 9 = 3 metres. Split at the turning point, the same integral gives 8 − 4 = 4 metres forwards from 0 to 2 seconds, and 3 − 4 = −1 metre from 2 to 3 seconds, which is 1 metre back.

The distance travelled adds the sizes of the two legs, 4 + 1 = 5 metres, and so it differs from the displacement of 3 metres. It is the [[total area|The size of every region between the graph and the axis, all counted positive. Met in 'When areas cancel'.]] of an earlier lesson applied to a velocity: split where the velocity changes sign, take the size of each part, and add.
The velocity 2t − 2 changes sign at t = 1. Split the trip there, take the size of each part, and add.
Combine the flows first, then integrate the net rate from 0 to 2.

lessons.orientation: Find how much a quantity has changed from the rate at which it changes, keeping track of the starting amount, the direction and the units.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A flow meter on a pipe reports litres per minute, and nobody wants that number for its own sake: what matters is how much water has passed. A speedometer reports metres per second, and what matters is how far the car has gone. In both cases the instrument measures a rate and the answer needed is an amount, which means going from the derivative back to the function, and the integral does exactly that.

Two details decide whether the answer is right. The amount at the end is the starting amount plus the change, so the integral alone is not enough; and when the rate has several parts, such as water flowing in and water flowing out, or a velocity that changes sign, they have to be combined with the right signs before the result can be trusted. This last lesson puts the whole course to work on those details.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a change from a net rate, add a starting amount to it, and tell displacement from distance travelled.

recap.keyIdea: The change in a quantity is the integral of its net rate, and the amount present is the starting amount plus that change.

blocks.text: To find how much has changed, integrate the net rate: combine inflow and outflow, or forward and backward velocity, into one signed rate, find an antiderivative, and subtract its values at the two ends. The amount present is the starting amount plus that change, and the units of the answer are the units of the rate multiplied by those of the input.

Displacement keeps the direction, while the distance travelled adds the sizes of the forward and backward parts. With this the two halves of the course meet: a derivative turns an amount into its rate, and an integral turns the rate back into the change in the amount.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x + 3, what value does f(x) approach as x approaches 2?
hints: Use inputs close to the stated point from both sides.
This line is continuous at the target input.
Insert the target input into x + 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nearby outputs approach 2 + 3 = 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. Outputs from both sides meet at 5, and that meeting point is the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 is where the input is heading. The question asks where the output goes.

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) as x approaches 3.
hints: Factor the difference of squares before considering the limit.
Write the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3).
Cancel the common factor for allowed nearby inputs, then approach the excluded input.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Factor the numerator as (x − 3)(x + 3). Away from 3 the quotient equals x + 3, which approaches 6.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Factor, cancel x − 3 for nearby x, then let x approach 3: 3 + 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 0/0 is not a value. Factor the top and cancel before letting x approach 3.
Factor the top as (x − 3)(x + 3) first, then cancel.

questions.prompt: The graph has f(x) = x + 1 for every x except 2, and f(2) = 5. Which statement is true?
hints: Follow the neighbouring points, not the isolated value at 2.

acceptedIdeas: The limit at 2 is 3
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Near 2 the graph follows the line y = x + 1, which approaches 3. Moving one point to 5 does not change the limit.

choices.label: The limit at 2 is 3
The limit at 2 is 5
There is no limit at 2

questions.onCorrect: Near 2 the graph follows the line y = x + 1, whose outputs head for 3. The single point at 5 sits off the line and does not change that.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is the value assigned at x = 2. The limit follows the neighbouring points instead.
One odd point does not stop the line around it from heading somewhere.

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 16)/(x − 4) as x approaches 4.
hints: Keep the excluded input in mind when you cancel the common factor.
Write the numerator as (x − 4)(x + 4).
Approach the excluded input in the remaining expression.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: For x ≠ 4 the quotient is x + 4, so its limit is 8.

questions.onCorrect: Cancelling the factor that causes the 0 ÷ 0 leaves x + 4, and 4 + 4 is the limit.

misconceptions.feedback: 0 ÷ 0 is not a value. Cancel the common factor first.
4 is where x is heading. Put it into what is left after cancelling.

questions.prompt: Find the limit of (x² − 25)/(x − 5) as x approaches 5.
hints: Recognise a difference of squares.
Factor the numerator as (x − 5)(x + 5).
Use the simplified expression only for the nearby inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The nearby expression is x + 5, which approaches 10.

questions.onCorrect: Cancel x − 5 and let x approach 5: the remaining x + 5 approaches 10.

misconceptions.feedback: Putting x = 5 straight in gives 0 ÷ 0, which is not a value. Cancel the common factor first.
5 is where x is heading. Put it into the cancelled expression, x + 5.

questions.prompt: Direct substitution in a quotient gives 0 ÷ 0. What should you do next?
hints: Both the top and the bottom approaching zero does not decide their ratio.

acceptedIdeas: Look at the quotient near the point, for instance by simplifying it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The form 0 ÷ 0 is indeterminate. Simplification or another valid method is needed.

choices.label: Look at the quotient near the point, for instance by simplifying it
Record 0 as the limit
Record 1 as the limit

questions.onCorrect: 0 ÷ 0 settles nothing. Look at what the quotient does near the point, for instance by cancelling a common factor.

misconceptions.feedback: Zero on top does not make the quotient zero when the bottom is zero as well.
A number divided by itself is 1 only when it is not zero, and here both are zero.

questions.prompt: A function equals 2 for x < 0 and 5 for x ≥ 0. What is its left-hand limit at 0?
hints: Which rule applies to inputs below 0?
The left-hand limit follows only those inputs.
Read the output that rule gives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Inputs below 0 give the output 2, so the left-hand limit is 2.

questions.onCorrect: Every input just below 0 gives the output 2, so that is where the left side arrives.

misconceptions.feedback: 5 is what the function gives at 0 and to its right. The left-hand limit follows only the inputs below 0.

questions.prompt: A function equals 2 for x < 0 and 5 for x ≥ 0. What is its right-hand limit at 0?
hints: Approach using only inputs greater than the target.
Use the branch whose condition is x ≥ 0.
Read the level followed by inputs just above the boundary.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Inputs above 0 stay on the horizontal level 5.

questions.onCorrect: 5. From the right, the graph stays on the level 5. The two sides head for different numbers.

misconceptions.feedback: 2 is the level on the left. The right-hand limit uses only inputs above 0.

questions.prompt: Near x = 1, f(x) = x + 2, but f(1) = 5. Is the function continuous at 1?
hints: Find the limit from the rule near 1, then compare it with f(1).

acceptedIdeas: No: the assigned value differs from the limit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The limit at 1 is 3, but the assigned value is 5, so the value does not match the limit.

choices.label: No: the assigned value differs from the limit
Yes: both sides have a limit
Yes: it is defined at the point

questions.onCorrect: The rule x + 2 leads the outputs to 3, while f(1) is 5. A value that differs from the limit breaks continuity.

misconceptions.feedback: Both sides having a limit is the second requirement only. The value at the point has to equal that limit as well.
Having a value is the first requirement only. The value also has to equal the limit.

questions.prompt: For x ≠ 2, f(x) = 2x + 4. What value must be assigned to f(2) for continuity?
hints: Continuity needs the value to equal the limit.
The limit comes from the rule 2x + 4 near 2.
Put x = 2 into that rule.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The surrounding rule approaches 2 × 2 + 4 = 8, so f(2) must be 8.

questions.onCorrect: The nearby outputs approach 2 × 2 + 4, and the assigned value must equal that limit.

misconceptions.feedback: 4 is the constant in 2x + 4. The limit comes from putting x = 2 into the whole rule.
2 is the point being approached. The value to assign is the number the outputs approach there.

questions.prompt: For x ≠ −1, g(x) = 3x + 7. Which numerical value at −1 makes g continuous?
hints: Continuity needs the value at −1 to equal the limit there.
The limit comes from the rule 3x + 7 near −1.
Put x = −1 into that rule and take care with the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The surrounding rule approaches 3 × (−1) + 7 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: The rule leads the outputs to 3 × (−1) + 7, and the assigned value must match it.

misconceptions.feedback: Take care with the sign when you put in −1: 3 × (−1) is negative.
7 is the constant in the rule. The limit comes from putting x = −1 into the whole rule.

questions.prompt: A function's left-hand limit at a point is 3 and its right-hand limit is 7. What is its two-sided limit there?
hints: A two-sided limit needs both sides to agree.

acceptedIdeas: It does not exist
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The sides lead to different numbers, so there is no two-sided limit.

choices.label: It does not exist
It equals their average
It equals the right-hand limit

questions.onCorrect: The sides lead to different numbers, so no single number is approached from both directions.

misconceptions.feedback: An average would suit a point halfway between the sides, but the outputs arrive at one number on the left and another on the right, and neither side is heading for the average.
The right-hand limit alone ignores the left, which heads for a different number. A two-sided limit has to account for both sides.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², find the average rate from x = 1 to x = 3.
hints: Work out f(1) and f(3).
Subtract them to get the change in the output.
Divide by the change in the input, 3 − 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f(3) = 9 and f(1) = 1, so the average rate is (9 − 1) ÷ (3 − 1) = 4.

questions.onCorrect: The output rises from 1 to 9, which is 8, over an interval of width 2.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 is the change in the output, 9 − 1. The average rate divides it by the change in the input as well.
2 is the width of the interval. The average rate divides the change in the output by it.

questions.prompt: At x = 2, the secant slope for f(x) = x² is 4 + h. What does it approach as h approaches 0?
hints: Which part of the expression depends on h?
That part shrinks towards zero.
What is left once it has gone?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: As h approaches 0, 4 + h approaches 4.

questions.onCorrect: The h term shrinks to nothing and the 4 does not depend on h, so the limit is 4.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the part containing h shrinks to nothing. The other part does not depend on h, so it stays.
2 is the point where the secant starts. The question asks for the number the slope approaches.

questions.prompt: How is a derivative at a point obtained from secant slopes?
hints: A height and a rate of change describe different things.

acceptedIdeas: Take their limit as the interval shrinks
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The derivative is the limiting slope, provided the limit exists.

choices.label: Take their limit as the interval shrinks
Substitute zero into the unsimplified denominator
Use the height of the graph

questions.onCorrect: Take the limit of the secant slopes. The limit avoids dividing by zero.

misconceptions.feedback: Putting h = 0 into the unsimplified quotient divides by zero. A limit gets round that.
A height and a rate are different things. The derivative is a slope.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², f′(x) = 2x. Find the instantaneous rate at x = 3.
hints: The instantaneous rate at a point is the derivative there.
The rule for the derivative is given: f′(x) = 2x.
Put x = 3 into it.
questions.onCorrect: The derivative at 3 is 2 × 3, which is smaller than the average rate over the unit that follows.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 is the average rate over the unit from 3 to 4. The instantaneous rate at 3 comes from the derivative 2x.
9 is the height f(3). The rate comes from the derivative 2x.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x², find the average rate from x = 2 to x = 5.
hints: Work out f(2) and f(5).
Subtract to get the change in the output.
Divide by 5 − 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f(5) = 25 and f(2) = 4, so the average rate is (25 − 4) ÷ (5 − 2) = 7.

questions.onCorrect: The output rises by 21 over an interval of width 3.

misconceptions.feedback: 21 is the change in the output, 25 − 4. The average rate divides it by the change in the input as well.
3 is the width of the interval. The average rate divides the change in the output by it.

questions.prompt: A function has f(2) = 9 and f′(2) = −3. Which statement describes its instantaneous rate at 2?
hints: The derivative gives the rate, not the height.

acceptedIdeas: It is falling at 3 output units per input unit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The derivative −3 is the instantaneous rate, so the function is falling at 3 output units per input unit.

Its height is negative three
It is rising at nine units per input unit

questions.onCorrect: The derivative f′(2) is the rate, and a negative rate means the output is falling as the input rises.

misconceptions.feedback: −3 is the derivative, a rate, and not a height. The height at 2 is given by f(2).
9 is the height f(2). The rate is the derivative, and it is negative, so the function is falling.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = x³, find f′(2).
hints: Bring the power down in front and lower the power by one.
That gives f′(x) = 3x².
Put x = 2 into f′(x).
questions.onCorrect: The derivative is 3x², and 3 × 2² is 12.

misconceptions.feedback: 8 is f(2), the height of the curve. The slope comes from the derivative, not from the function.
3 × 2 forgets to lower the power. The derivative is 3 times x to a lower power.

questions.prompt: For g(x) = 2x² + 5, find g′(1).
hints: Differentiate 2x² first, then deal with the constant.
The derivative is 4x.
Put x = 1 into it.
questions.onCorrect: The constant disappears, and the derivative 4x gives its slope at 1.

misconceptions.feedback: 7 is g(1), the height of the curve. The slope comes from the derivative.
2 is the multiple only. The power rule also brings down the power on x.

questions.prompt: Which expression is the derivative of 3x² − 2x + 7?
hints: Differentiate 3x² first, then −2x, then the constant 7.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Differentiate term by term: 3x² gives 6x, −2x gives −2, and the constant 7 gives 0.

questions.onCorrect: The three terms give 6x, −2 and 0, and together they make 6x − 2.

misconceptions.feedback: The 7 is a constant, and a constant has slope 0, so it vanishes from the derivative instead of staying.
3x leaves out the power: the derivative of x² is 2x, and the multiple 3 then applies, so the first term is 6x.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = 4 − x², find f′(1).
hints: The constant 4 contributes nothing.
The term −x² differentiates to −2x.
Put x = 1 into the result.
questions.onCorrect: The derivative is −2x, and a negative slope fits a curve that is falling at 1.

misconceptions.feedback: The minus sign in front of x² stays through the rule, so the derivative of −x² is negative.
3 is f(1), the height of the curve. The slope comes from the derivative.

questions.prompt: For p(x) = 2x³ − 5x + 9, find p′(2).
hints: Differentiate each term: 2x³, then −5x, then 9.
The derivative is 6x² − 5.
Put x = 2 into it.

misconceptions.feedback: 15 is p(2), the height of the curve. The slope comes from the derivative.
24 comes from the cubic term alone. The term −5x contributes a slope of its own.

questions.prompt: Adding 10 to a differentiable function changes its derivative in which way?
hints: Think about what adding a constant does to the shape of the graph.

acceptedIdeas: It leaves the derivative unchanged
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Adding 10 lifts the graph without changing its steepness, so every slope stays the same.

choices.label: It leaves the derivative unchanged
It adds ten to every slope
It multiplies every slope by ten

questions.onCorrect: Raising the graph by 10 moves it up and leaves every tangent with the slope it had.

misconceptions.feedback: A slope measures steepness, and lifting the graph does not make it steeper. The derivative of a constant is zero, so nothing is added.
Multiplying the function by 10 would multiply the slopes by 10. Adding 10 only shifts the graph upwards.

questions.prompt: For f(x) = (2x + 1)², find f′(1).
hints: Name the inner function 2x + 1 and the outer function that squares it.
The derivative is the outer derivative at the inner value, times the inner rate.
Put x = 1 into the result.
